\title{\Large \textsc{Estimating Spain's income distribution from neighborhood-level data}}

\author{\href{https://pablogguz.github.io/}{\large{Pablo García-Guzmán}\thanks{Email: \href{mailto:garciagp@ebrd.com}{garciagp@ebrd.com}. I thank Pedro Torres for his valuable feedback and comments. The code and replication package for this note are available at \href{https://github.com/pablogguz/compara_tu_ingreso_app}{github.com/pablogguz/compara\_tu\_ingreso\_app}.}} \\ \normalsize{}}

\maketitle
\begin{abstract}
\onehalfspacing
This methodology note develops a transparent and simple framework to estimate aggregate income distributions in Spain exploiting the availability of granular inequality metrics. Specifically, I leverage distributional indicators derived from personal income-tax records at the census tract-level to reconstruct local income distributions assuming a generalized beta distribution of the second kind (GB2). National, regional and municipal income distributions can be subsequently derived as population-weighted mixtures of these tract-level distributions. This approach leverages well-documented regularities in how incomes are distributed within demographically homogeneous groups, and the resulting estimates closely match observed distributional statistics in validation tests: the national shares of the population below nine published income thresholds are reproduced within \ThrAllMaxDiff{} percentage points. While the focus is on Spain, the approach uses only published small-area statistics and can be readily adapted to other countries with comparable data available. The framework is implemented in \href{https://comparatuingreso.es/}{\mbox{comparatuingreso.es}}, a publicly available web platform that enables Spanish households to calculate their relative position within the income distribution.
\end{abstract}

\thispagestyle{empty}

\section{Introduction}

Understanding the income distribution is crucial for economic analysis and policy design, yet its measurement remains challenging. Statistical offices increasingly publish income statistics for small geographic units, such as mean and median incomes, inequality indices and the shares of the population below given income levels, but rarely the full distributions behind them, and how to recover those distributions from published summary statistics has received little attention. In this note, I propose a transparent and simple method to do so. The approach builds on two insights: first, that the income distribution of a small, demographically homogeneous area can be well described by a flexible parametric family fitted to the statistics published for it; and second, that the distribution of any larger area can then be obtained as a population-weighted mixture of these local distributions.

I apply the method to Spain, where the Spanish Statistical Office publishes a set of distributional indicators derived from personal income-tax records for each of its \TractsTotal{} census tracts, the smallest areas for which official statistics are released, with \TractPopMean{} residents on average. I model each tract's distribution as a generalized beta distribution of the second kind (GB2), a four-parameter family that nests the log-normal as a limiting case, fitted to these indicators. The resulting national, provincial and municipal distributions closely match the statistics published for those levels, which are not used in the estimation: the national median falls inside its published interval, the Gini coefficients of provinces and municipalities are reproduced within \ProvGiniAbsErr{} and \MunGiniAbsErr{} points on average, and the national shares of the population below nine published income thresholds within \ThrAllMaxDiff{} percentage points. The method is implemented in \href{https://comparatuingreso.es/}{\mbox{comparatuingreso.es}}, a publicly available web platform that enables Spanish households to calculate their relative position within the income distribution of Spain, their province and their municipality.

The rest of this note is organized as follows. Section \ref{sec:data} describes the data sources, their coverage and scope. Section \ref{sec:method} outlines the methodology, including the modeling of local income distributions and their aggregation. Section \ref{sec:results} presents the validation results and a decomposition of income inequality. Finally, Section \ref{sec:conc} concludes.

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conc}

This note has described a transparent way to estimate income distributions for Spain, its provinces and its municipalities from tract-level statistics: fit a GB2 to the thirteen statistics published for each tract, and aggregate tracts into population-weighted mixtures. Out of sample, the resulting distributions reproduce published medians, Gini coefficients and P80/P20 ratios closely at every level, and the national shares below income thresholds within \ThrOtherMaxDiff{} percentage points above \texteuro 5,000.

Their main limitation is the lowest incomes: the model places \ThrFiveKModel{}\% of the population below \texteuro 5,000 per consumption unit, against \ThrFiveKObs{}\%, and so slightly understates the position of the poorest households. Other limitations are smaller or affect few users. The top of the distribution rests on the GB2's Pareto tail beyond the highest published threshold and on tract medians that the ADRH caps. The distributions of the smallest municipalities rest on imputed inputs and a log-normal. The two-year nowcast has missed the published income level by \NowcastBtMAE{} percentage points on average in the past. Finally, the ADRH measures income recorded by the tax authorities, which includes remuneration in kind and notional income from second homes and excludes informal earnings and transfers between households, whereas users report the money that reaches their household.

Natural extensions are a component for very low incomes within each tract, to close the remaining gap below \texteuro 5,000, and the use of external information on top incomes to discipline the upper tail. The framework can be adapted to other countries with comparable small-area data.
